findings.title: A pool whose hook address has no code on its own network freezes every position when the address sets a removal flag, and live pools on Polygon and Avalanche hold third-party positions frozen this way
findings.difference: No opcode difference: on all 21 networks a call to an address without code returns success and no data (measured). The networks differ only in which hook addresses are empty: the hook 0xf8c3f4243c4d8c02831a718a7978fd869f094300 (bits 9 and 8) has 2,488 bytes of code on Ethereum, OP Mainnet, Base, Unichain and Arbitrum One and none on Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, World Chain and Avalanche, because it was deployed through the CREATE2 deployer 0x4e59b44847b379578588920ca78fbf26c0b4956c on some networks only, and pool creators on the others named the same address.
findings.mechanism: 1. initialize checks only the low 14 bits of the hook address and never reads its code (src/PoolManager.sol:126, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-127). 2. For liquidityDelta <= 0, beforeModifyLiquidity calls beforeRemoveLiquidity when bit 9 is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:203-204) and afterModifyLiquidity calls afterRemoveLiquidity when bit 8 is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:232-243); donate calls the donate hooks for bits 5 and 4 (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:317-335). 3. callHook makes a plain CALL with all gas (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134). An address without code returns success and no data, so result.length < 32 and the call reverts with InvalidHookResponse (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152-154). The only bypass is msg.sender == hook (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:171-175, 217), which nobody holds for an empty address. 4. This cycle measured the call on all 21 networks: an eth_call from each PoolManager address with beforeRemoveLiquidity calldata to three seeded random addresses, to 0x...20, to 0x...dead0030 and to every empty hook address of that network returned success with empty data in all 199 calls (raw/emptycall.json), so the freeze has the same shape everywhere. 5. findings.impact: Principal and fees of every position in such a pool, for every holder. Measured third-party exposure is dust: on Polygon about 0.019 POL and 0.0015 USDC across two positions, on Avalanche about 0.045 AVAX and 0.32 USDt across six positions, and nothing on BNB Smart Chain and Base, where the pools on 0xf8c3f424...4300 hold only the positions of their creators. No funds outside these pools are reachable, because the deltas of a removal only involve the pool's own currencies and its hook.
findings.preconditions: A pool creator names a flagged address that has no code on that network, and other accounts add liquidity. No role is needed for either step. The third-party owners in the Polygon and Avalanche pools are smart accounts and EOAs that also create pools on the same hooks, so they may be one operator; that link was not established.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces and routers should read the code at the hook address on the network itself before listing a pool or adding liquidity, and should not infer it from another network. Core could reject an empty hook address in initialize, which would not stop later loss of code (F-013).

findings.title: Hook addresses that are EIP-7702 delegated accounts are live on five networks, their holders have repointed them, and one Ethereum pool whose delegated hook sets the after remove liquidity and return delta flags holds a third-party position
findings.difference: On the networks listed, a hook address can be an EOA whose code is a 23 byte delegation indicator 0xef0100 followed by a target address, which its holder can change or clear in any later transaction. Measured: 0x12c220215d4c232a45fd815b37fadb6125bfe58b on Ethereum (nonce 1, delegate 0xa7acb7b7), Robinhood Chain (nonce 1, delegate 0x60ea7062); 0x17da3aa3d761ff479277d18c5a11a041a2b2e58b on Ethereum (nonce 1, delegate 0xcd1cbc5d), Base (nonce 2, delegate 0x8e22edf8); 0x30a5640e16c987e070ac2e8e1695df096d22658b on Base (nonce 6, delegate 0x5b81c61b); 0x52bf1a8075581c2e40854d3ece7181e1fb41258b on Ethereum (nonce 11, delegate 0x1154ae56), Base (nonce 5, delegate 0x8a877682), Arbitrum One (nonce 1, delegate 0xce9689d9), Robinhood Chain (nonce 2, delegate 0x60ea7062), BNB Smart Chain (nonce 3, delegate 0xff04024b); 0x8c7852bb503b4579c28a6fa2bcf112c7657a6488 on BNB Smart Chain (nonce 2, delegate 0x61a35fd5); 0xa853180523bd16fa6a9c449ab050e108da642488 on Ethereum (nonce 9, delegate 0x16765af6), Base (nonce 3, delegate 0x30f2ad79), Arbitrum One (nonce 1, delegate 0x1947e2c7), Robinhood Chain (nonce 1, delegate 0x3620c36b), BNB Smart Chain (nonce 6, delegate 0x3fe96d6f); 0xf028a2640078ffd41078e1f2e5a6425cc83d658b on Ethereum (nonce 1, delegate 0x20d737a8). The same hook address points at different targets on different networks, so the holders have set the delegation per network.
findings.mechanism: initialize accepts any address whose low 14 bits form a valid flag set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-127). Bits 0x258b mean before initialize, after add liquidity, after remove liquidity, before swap, before swap returns delta, after add liquidity returns delta and after remove liquidity returns delta. With bit 8 and bit 0 the hook delta returned by afterRemoveLiquidity is subtracted from the remover's delta without bound and credited to the hook (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:232-243, src/PoolManager.sol:177-183), and with no code at all every removal reverts (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152-154). The holder of the hook account can therefore repoint the delegation to code that takes all of a removal, or clear it to freeze removals. Live pools on delegated hooks with liquidity: Ethereum pool 0x08834f721b53ef87 (hook 0xa8531805, bits 0x2488, creator 0xec08eff7): 2 live positions, 1 of other accounts (token 514342 of 0x3d4e4f78 holding 0.005484 native and 0.03799 USDC); Ethereum pool 0x992c0ab607f40131 (hook 0x52bf1a80, bits 0x258b, creator 0xec08eff7): 2 live positions, 1 of other accounts (token 517545 of 0x3d4e4f78 holding 0.003502 native and 0 USDC); Ethereum pool 0xc73d0691a937b5e3 (hook 0xf028a264, bits 0x258b, creator 0xec08eff7): 1 live positions, 0 of other accounts; Arbitrum One pool 0xa8382d4ecf92967d (hook 0x52bf1a80, bits 0x258b, creator 0xec08eff7): 1 live positions, 0 of other accounts; Robinhood Chain pool 0xbbb6d0064ae13826 (hook 0xa8531805, bits 0x2488, creator 0xec08eff7): 1 live positions, 0 of other accounts; Robinhood Chain pool 0x9230716faece51bb (hook 0x52bf1a80, bits 0x258b, creator 0xec08eff7): 1 live positions, 0 of other accounts; BNB Smart Chain pool 0xc4fe2e50daa48e0d (hook 0xa8531805, bits 0x2488, creator 0xec08eff7): 1 live positions, 0 of other accounts; BNB Smart Chain pool 0x4ab42853cc758432 (hook 0x8c7852bb, bits 0x2488, creator 0xec08eff7): 1 live positions, 0 of other accounts; BNB Smart Chain pool 0x822e43b5560c8bc3 (hook 0x52bf1a80, bits 0x258b, creator 0xec08eff7): 1 live positions, 0 of other accounts.
findings.impact: Removal proceeds of the third-party positions in pools on delegated hooks with bits 8 and 0, measured on Ethereum at about 0.0035 ETH in pool 0x992c0ab6. Swappers in pools with the before swap returns delta flag. No other pools.
findings.preconditions: The victim adds liquidity to a pool whose hook address is a delegated EOA. Only the holder of that account, the hook author, can act.
findings.mitigations: Routers and interfaces should treat a hook whose code starts with 0xef0100 as mutable and warn or refuse.

cleared.check: Lead L-953: which rows, clearances and findings rest on the cycle 17 hook census (hooks7702.json) and the cycle 5 Initialize scan that fed it.
cleared.result: The cycle 5 scan stores rows as [block, pool id topic, currency0, currency1, fee, tickSpacing, hooks, transaction hash] (cycles/005/theme-shared-hooks.work/init_census.py:36). hooks7702.py read index 7, the transaction hash, as the pool id for the StateView.getLiquidity call and for the poolId field (cycles/017/ethereum-reference.work/hooks7702.py:42 and 45); its hook selection used index 6 and is correct (line 11). So every one of its 21 rows has a wrong poolId and a liquidity reading taken at an unused slot, and its counts of empty and delegated hooks are right for its block. The census stored only those 21 rows; it never read liquidity for pools on hooks with code, so no other row exists to be wrong. What rests on the wrong fields: cleared entry 1489 (cycle 17, also CLEARED.md line 351), the cycle 17 attempt of lead L-046 in ledger.json, the sentence in OPCODES.md line 345 that the 21 pools give no third party a path to funds, and cycle 21 l821.py, which recomputed the ids itself and is correct (cleared 1811). The other readers of the cycle 5 and cycle 6 rows (cycles/005/theme-shared-hooks.work/summ.py:29, klik_frozen_pools.py:17-19, cycles/006/theme-currency-lists.work/census2.py:40, lists.py:27-29, cycles/022/theme-outflow-census.work/census3.py:22) index the rows by field 1 and use field 7 only as a transaction hash. Cleared entries 658 to 678 use only the hook addresses. With the ids recomputed, the Ethereum answer is now 24 pools on 21 hooks (16 empty, 5 delegated) at block 26,496,175; on two of them other accounts hold positions, both on delegated hooks (finding F-013 above). The pool on an empty hook with bit 9 holds only its creator's position (F-004).

The special ranges found earlier change the outcome only for addresses that no pool uses: BNB Smart Chain CAS20 ordinals 0x00 and 0x01 and three fixed addresses revert every call after Jenner (F-139), which still freezes a pool flagged for them, and Arc fails only value-carrying calls (F-125), which hook calls are not (value 0 at src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134). cleared.check: Task 3: who can place code at 0xf8c3f4243c4d8c02831a718a7978fd869f094300 on the networks where it is empty, and does that account gain control of the removal callbacks.
cleared.result: Anyone can place code there, and nobody gains control. On Ethereum the address was created at block 21,696,306 by transaction 0x7311a22f...2811 from 0xb7a249bd to the CREATE2 deployer 0x4e59b448 with salt 0x...0492 and 3,272 bytes of init code; keccak256(0xff ++ 0x4e59b448... ++ salt ++ keccak256(initcode)) reproduces the address. The deployer has its 69 byte code on Polygon, Avalanche, BNB Smart Chain and World Chain, and the original call carries no signature of its own, so any account can send the same call there and get the same 2,488 byte runtime, because the address commits to the init code. That runtime has no SSTORE, SLOAD or ORIGIN; it keeps the Ethereum PoolManager address 0x000000000004444c5dc75cb358380d2e3de08a90 as an immutable, checks CALLER against it (PC 0x37b to 0x3aa), and answers beforeRemoveLiquidity with HookNotImplemented (0x0a85dc29) on Ethereum, Base and OP Mainnet. eth_call of the third-party removals with that runtime placed at the hook address by state override reverts with WrappedError(0xf8c3..., 0x21d0ee70, HookNotImplemented, HookCallFailed) in all 8 runs on Polygon and Avalanche, so the pools stay frozen after a replay. Other code cannot reach the address: a CREATE2 or CREATE output equal to a fixed 160 bit address, or the signing secret of a CREATE2 output, needs about 2^160 work. The address has nonce 0 on all four networks.

cleared.check: Task 3: pools on 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000020 (bit 5) and 0x00000000000000000000000000000000dead0030 (bits 5 and 4) that hold third-party positions, on Robinhood Chain pools 0x4996584f... and 0x7d10f8e6....
cleared.result: No freeze of principal. These flags gate only donate (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:317-335); removal and swaps call no hook (bits 9, 8, 7, 6 unset). Donate to such a pool reverts, which takes nothing from LPs. Nobody can place code at either address: both have nonce 0 and no code on all 21 networks (raw/xchain.json), neither is a precompile or system address on any of them (raw/emptycall.json answers success and empty data), and producing a CREATE or CREATE2 output or a signing secret for a fixed address needs about 2^160 work.

cleared.check: Whether the permissionless deterministic factories that a hook deployed on one network could be replayed through exist on all 21 networks.
cleared.result: Yes. The CREATE2 deployer 0x4e59b44847b379578588920ca78fbf26c0b4956c has its 69 byte code and CreateX 0xba5ed099633d3b313e4d5f7bdc1305d3c28ba5ed its 11,838 byte code on all 21 networks. So a hook address made through 0x4e59b448 or through CreateX CREATE2 on one network can be filled on any other by whoever has the init code, and what that account controls is decided by the init code alone. A CreateX CREATE3 address does not depend on the init code, so when its salt does not carry the deployer in its first 20 bytes (the permissioned deploy protection in the CreateX README) any account can place any code at it on another network. Of the 82 hook addresses in use that are empty on some network, 25 have contract code on another network (raw/xchain.json); only 0xf8c3f424...4300 among them sets bit 9, 8, 5 or 4, and it is cleared above.
cleared.source: research/network-risk/cycles/022/theme-empty-hook-pools.work/raw/factories.json, raw/xchain.json; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pcaversaccio/createx/main/README.md (Permissioned Deploy Protection and Cross-Chain Redeploy Protection, lines 576 and 709-734 of the fetched copy)

leads.why: Such a replay would give an ordinary account the swap callbacks and return deltas of pools that other accounts trade in. Removal stays open in these pools, so LP principal is not at stake, which is why this was not followed here.
